title: Wolves enter Finnish villages after Google clears 1300 acres for AI data centers
content:
Wolves roam into Finnish villages after Google destroys 1,300 acres of forest for AI data centers — forest where wolf packs used to live is now an expanse of mud
This is thankfully a less common but still very serious side effect of an AI data center being built nearby.
Google’s Finland country manager has apologized for unauthorized forest clearings near Muhos, which have turned 816 acres of forest into an expanse of mud. The American search and AI giant has also been told to cease work where it has cleared roughly 500 acres of forest, 55 miles southeast of the village of Otanmäki. Now The Guardian reports that wolves, who used to live in the forests, are roaming into villages neighboring these man-made muddy wastelands.
Local anger continues to simmer over the damage done to Finnish forests, as Google seems to have ridden roughshod over regulations in the hurry to build new AI data centers in Finland. However, the report suggests that it isn’t just environmentalists who have a beef with Google. Some families say wolves and other wild animals have entered the countryside villages. This would be a serious human safety concern.
“We had wolves coming into the village because all the wild animals moved out of the forest,” explained Anni Ranta, 53, whose family has lived in Otanmäki for generations. Ranta also fears the U.S.-owned data centers will make Finland an even juicier target for Russian aggression.
Finland is far from the first place targeted by AI data center developers to complain about environmental effects. This latest report also cites locals grumbling about construction/factory noise, streams turning brown, and rare birds being pushed out, among other unwanted side effects. We’ve seen similar concerns voiced across the U.S. and in other countries.
Google’s flouting of environmental policy has been unprecedented and clear, a representative of the Finnish Association for Nature Conservation (SLL) indicated to The Guardian. The Finnish Licensing and Supervision Authority (LVV) seems to agree, as it issued an order for Google to stop development near Muhos and Otanmäki. Nevertheless, a Google spokesperson was upbeat. “We will fully comply with LVV’s requests in this matter,” they said. “We look forward to maintaining an active, open dialogue with all authorities to strengthen our partnership with Finland and local organizations.” Google must be hoping the touted business benefits of the data centers will sway the government and/or regulators.
We last reported on these in-development data centers in Finland earlier this month, after the Finnish government (LVV) gave notice to Google to stop its construction activities in Muhos and Kajaani (near Otanmäki).

report.summary: Google cleared hundreds of acres of Finnish forest for AI data centers without proper permits, and displaced wolves are now wandering into nearby villages, prompting regulators to halt work.
report.background: Finland has become a magnet for hyperscale data centers thanks to cool climates that cut cooling costs, abundant renewable power, and a grid that dates back to Google's 2011 Hamina conversion of a former paper mill. As the AI boom supercharged demand for compute, Google expanded aggressively around Muhos, Kajaani and Otanmäki. But forest clearance outpaced permitting: Finland's Licensing and Supervision Authority (LVV) found work proceeding without required approvals, and Google's country manager has publicly apologized. Northern forests are also sensitive habitat for wolf packs, whose displacement has turned a permitting dispute into a human-safety story. The episode mirrors tensions across the US, Ireland and the Netherlands, where data center growth is colliding with land, water and power limits.
key_points: Unpermitted clearing: Around 816 acres of forest near Muhos were reduced to mud, and roughly 500 acres more near Otanmäki were cleared before Finland's LVV regulator ordered Google to halt construction, citing regulatory violations.

Wildlife pushed into towns: With their forest habitat gone, wolves and other animals have moved into villages such as Otanmäki. Residents describe the animals entering the village directly, raising concerns about livestock, pets and human safety.

Beyond wolves: Locals also report construction noise, streams turning brown from runoff, and rare bird populations being displaced, echoing complaints already common around data center buildouts in the US and Europe.

Corporate response: Google apologized and said it will 'fully comply' with LVV's orders while emphasizing dialogue with authorities, betting that the economic benefits of the facilities will keep the Finnish government onside.
A wider pattern: The dispute illustrates how AI's compute rush is running into environmental permitting and land-use limits, even in countries that actively court data center investment.
report.impact: For the AI industry, this is a reminder that the compute buildout's bottleneck is increasingly political and environmental rather than technical. Companies that treat permitting as paperwork risk construction halts, reputational damage and stricter rules in exactly the regions offering cheap, green power. For developers, delays upstream can translate into capacity constraints and pricing pressure on cloud GPU rentals. For regular users, the story connects everyday AI features to real-world costs — forests, wildlife and local trust. Expect regulators and communities to demand earlier consultation, biodiversity assessments and transparent water and land use, and expect 'green data center' claims to face much sharper scrutiny.
report.tools: To follow land-use and forest-loss claims, try Global Forest Watch and Google Earth Engine for satellite-based tree-cover alerts, Sentinel Hub for free Sentinel-2 imagery of specific sites, and OpenStreetMap for mapping nearby infrastructure. For tracking data center expansion generally, Data Center Map and the IEA's electricity-and-data-centre reports are useful references, alongside national regulators' permit databases such as Finland's LVV.
